topic: UX for map-centric field/emergency-management and GIS web apps: list-map synchronization, maps on small screens (full-screen map + bottom sheet vs split view), legends and layer toggles, evidence/photo markers, when to hide the map and show a list, and 3D scene viewers on tablets - applied to the ERIS (Caltrans geotechnical emergency response) web app

findings.principle: Split view (results list beside a live map) is the layout users actually engage with. In Baymard's accommodation-search testing, 65% of users on list-view-default sites never engaged the map because they could not find the map toggle, while 95% engaged the map when a split view was shown; users also used map zoom as a geographic filter while keeping the list visible. Baymard's three pitfalls: overlay presentations that users mistake for the full page (hiding sort/filter controls), vertical filter sidebars that crowd the list, and vertical side content that steals width.
findings.applicability: The coordinator triage queue and the chief routing queue on desktop and iPad landscape should be a persistent two-pane split view (incident/assessment list + map), not a list with a 'Map' tab. Put triage filters (district, status, priority, date) in a horizontal filter bar above the list, and render incident detail in a docked side panel rather than a modal overlay so sort/filter controls stay visible.

findings.principle: Esri's dashboard model formalizes list-map synchronization as configurable actions: when a list row is selected, the map can 'zoom, pan, flash, show pop-up, and follow feature'; when the map is the source, 'a change in the map's extent can filter one or more elements on the dashboard'. The Emergency Management Operations solution applies this so that 'if you click an incident in the Incidents list or zoom to a location on the map, related details are filtered and updated in other elements', and uses an 'Active Incident' boolean to control which features appear on internal maps.
findings.applicability: Implement bidirectional sync with these exact semantics: selecting a list row pans and flashes/highlights the marker (avoid aggressive zoom on every selection); clicking a marker scrolls its row into view and highlights it; an explicit 'Filter list to map area' toggle applies the current extent as a spatial filter to the list and to status-count indicators. Model an 'active' flag so closed/resolved incidents are hidden from the coordinator map by default (see also https://doc.arcgis.com/en/arcgis-solutions/latest/reference/use-emergency-management-operations.htm and https://doc.arcgis.com/en/dashboards/latest/get-started/map-element-and-tools.htm).

findings.principle: Esri's 'Author effective dashboards' guidance: 'A good first step ... is to determine who is viewing it, and the questions they need answered'; 'The elements with the most important information should be the largest and have the most prominent locations'; 'Use element grouping for related elements'; 'A common design issue in dashboards is the overuse of color'; 'Using a selection-based display can be an effective way of ensuring that users have the appropriate context'; and 'include no more than two notifications in a dashboard'.
findings.applicability: ERIS has distinct audiences with distinct questions (coordinator: what is new and urgent; chief: what needs routing; reviewer: what awaits approval; engineer: my assigned assessments). Build role-specific home views rather than one shared mega-dashboard. Make the detail panel selection-driven with an empty state ('Select an incident to see details'), group the map with its legend, keep status color to a single restrained palette, and cap persistent banners/alerts at two.

findings.principle: For phone-sized dashboard views Esri recommends: 'keep the design simple', 'limit the amount of data and visualizations', 'A dashboard's mobile view should have a maximum of one map' with 'one operational layer, with a minimum number of features', 'Disable pop-ups on a map's operational layers' because tapping small features is difficult, prefer 'Indicators and gauges' that 'can be understood quickly', and use stacking so 'Stacking creates a tabbed view of the elements' - but 'be conservative' and do not recreate the desktop layout on a phone.
findings.applicability: On phones ERIS should default to a list-first triage screen with status-count chips (indicators), and offer a single map tab showing only the incident layer. Do not depend on map popups on phones; tapping a marker should open a bottom sheet. Keep cross-sections, 3D terrain and multi-layer analysis off the phone view entirely.

findings.principle: NN/g defines the bottom sheet as an overlay anchored to the bottom edge used for progressive disclosure, and distinguishes modal sheets (block background) from nonmodal sheets that 'allow continued interaction with background content' - the ideal pattern for maps, as in Google Maps where destination details show while the user pans and zooms. Guidelines: allow Back to dismiss, 'Include a Close Button' (swipe-only dismissal is error-prone and inaccessible), 'Do Not Stack Bottom Sheets', and use sheets for short interactions, not lengthy content.
findings.applicability: On phones and iPad portrait, selecting an incident marker should open a nonmodal bottom sheet with the incident summary (ID, route/postmile, priority, status, first photo) and a primary 'Open full report' action that navigates to a full page. Give the sheet a visible close button and support hardware/browser Back. Never nest sheets and never put the GISA form or the routing/approval workflow inside a sheet.

findings.principle: Esri's Calcite Design System separates persistent and ephemeral containers: 'Shell Panels can be open and persist ... indefinitely' and 'should be displayed alongside visible and interactive primary application content' (controls, filters, legends), whereas Sheet and Dialog are modal and block the map while open. 'On narrow viewports, such as a mobile device, use Sheet with the position property set to block-end to improve touch interactions'; avoid opening multiple Sheets; and adapt by rendering content in a Dialog on large screens but a Sheet on mobile, or moving Shell Panels between slots 'based on screen size'.
findings.applicability: Layer toggles, legend and filters belong in a collapsible start-side panel on desktop/iPad landscape (stays open while the map is used), and the same content becomes a block-end (bottom) sheet on narrow viewports. Do not present the legend or layer list as a modal dialog over the map. Use an action bar on the map edge to open/close these panels (see also https://developers.arcgis.com/calcite-design-system/foundations/layouts/).

findings.principle: Legends should mirror what is actually visible: 'If a layer's visibility is hidden in the web map legend, it is hidden in the legend element' and 'if a layer is not visible ... due to scale range thresholds, it does not appear in the legend element'. A legend is 'particularly useful when the map has multiple operational or thematic layers', and you do not need to show reference layers in it. The Maps SDK Legend's respectLayerVisibility (default true) implements this: legend entries are not rendered when legendEnabled is false or the view scale is outside the layer's minScale/maxScale.
findings.applicability: The ERIS legend should list only operational symbols (incident priority/status, assessment state, evidence photo marker) and omit basemap and reference layers; it must update live as layer toggles change and as scale-dependent layers drop out. Keep the legend adjacent to (grouped with) the map. Reference: https://developers.arcgis.com/javascript/latest/api-reference/esri-widgets-Legend.html

findings.principle: NN/g: 'The problem with legends is that they require people to quickly look back and forth between the data visualization and the legend', direct labeling is 'easier for people to process', and 'It's difficult for people with certain visual impairments - particularly people who are colorblind - to rely on color alone to differentiate between data series.'
findings.applicability: Encode incident priority and workflow status with shape + color + a short text label (marker glyph or numeric badge; text chips in list rows) so the legend is a backup, not a prerequisite. Status chips in the list and detail panel must carry text ('Awaiting routing', 'In review'), never color alone.

findings.principle: NN/g toggle-switch guidance: 'Toggle switches are best used for changing the state of system functionalities and preferences', 'Toggle switches should take immediate effect and should not require the user to click Save or Submit', and labels should be 'short and direct' describing the on state; if immediate effect is not possible, use checkboxes or radio buttons.
findings.applicability: Layer visibility controls in ERIS are true toggles: flipping 'Show closed incidents' or 'Show assessment routes' updates the map instantly with no Apply button, and labels name the on state (not questions). Attribute filters that are meant to be combined and applied together (district, date range) should be checkboxes/selects with an explicit Apply, not switches.

findings.principle: Esri's clustering guidance: clustering 'should only be used as a visualization technique to reduce visual clutter because of many overlapping features or to provide a quick preview of feature density', 'should not be used as a means of performing statistical analysis', clusters should be labeled with a rounded/abbreviated count, and cluster popups can summarize the aggregated features (cluster_count).
findings.applicability: Cluster incident markers only at statewide/district zoom where markers overlap, label clusters with counts, and let a cluster tap either zoom in or list the incidents inside it. Disable clustering at site/assessment scale where engineers and reviewers need exact positions of evidence photo markers and boring/observation points. Never derive status counts from clusters; compute them from the filtered dataset.

findings.principle: Esri Field Maps places photo capture inside the form: attachment elements 'can be placed anywhere in a form', 'can be shown or hidden based on form values', and 'can require a minimum or maximum number of attachments before the form can be submitted'; workers can 'Take Photo' or 'Choose Photo'. Because 'If photos are large, they can quickly increase the size of the database' and 'Attaching smaller photos means less data to store and faster sync times', Field Maps resizes photos (default large 960x1280). In popups, AttachmentsContent displayType 'preview' 'Shows a thumbnail image of the attachment' while 'list' 'Shows a list of attachment links'.
findings.applicability: In the GISA form, put photo capture blocks next to the questions they evidence (slope face, drainage, roadway damage) with per-section minimum counts where evidence is mandatory, and show them conditionally (e.g., only when 'retaining structure present' is Yes). Resize client-side to roughly 960x1280 before upload on iPads, keep originals optional. Render photos as numbered thumbnail (preview) markers on the site map and in the detail panel/popup; show PDFs/reports as a link list. See also https://doc.arcgis.com/en/field-maps/latest/prepare-maps/configure-the-map.htm and https://developers.arcgis.com/javascript/latest/references/core/popup/content/AttachmentsContent/

findings.principle: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8: 'The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels', with exceptions including 'Equivalent: The function can be achieved through a different control on the same page that meets this criterion' and 'Essential'. W3C explicitly discusses maps: 'If there are many pins close together, the spacing between pins ... will often be below 24 CSS pixels. It is essential to show the pins at the correct map location, therefore the Essential exception applies.'
findings.applicability: Dense incident pins are allowed under the Essential exception, but ERIS should still satisfy the Equivalent path by always providing the synchronized list as a conforming way to select any incident. All map chrome (zoom, locate, layer toggle, legend, basemap) and list rows should be at least 24x24 CSS px, and 44x44 on iPad/touch surfaces used in the field.

findings.principle: W3C WAI's Accessible Maps research summary: many applications 'use visual maps to communicate location based information to the user, which is a problem for people suffering from visual disabilities or blindness', and 'the information on a visual map usually is very compressed'; accessible approaches rely on alternative, structured (text/audio/tactile) representations of the same information rather than the visual map alone.
findings.applicability: Every ERIS map view must have an equivalent list/table exposing the same records, sort and filters (route, postmile, county, status), and every workflow step - triage, routing, review/approval, admin - must be completable without touching the map. Map markers should be keyboard-focusable with the list as the primary keyboard path; the map is an accelerator, not the sole access route.

findings.principle: 3D on tablets is constrained. ArcGIS Scene Viewer requires 'WebGL2-enabled, 64-bit browsers', supports 'Safari on iPhone and iPad Pro series', and 'Mobile devices must have a minimum of 6 GB RAM' plus 'a powerful multicore CPU and GPU'. The Maps SDK for JavaScript requires 'Mobile devices - at least 4 GB system memory', and its SceneView 'qualityProfile is evaluated and set automatically when SceneView loads depending on the detected device'; 'In most scenarios it is recommended to not set qualityProfile'; 'Applications should also consider providing an option to change the quality profile'; the default is 'low for all browsers on iPhones'; when memory limits are approached the view reduces level of detail and feature counts.
findings.applicability: Treat the 3D terrain/cross-section scene as progressive enhancement: gate it behind a WebGL2 + device-memory check, never auto-load it on phones, and fall back to the 2D map plus a rendered cross-section image when unsupported or when loading stalls (with visible progress and a timeout - relevant to the recent 'scenes stuck at loading' fix). Leave qualityProfile on auto but expose a 'Quality: Auto / Low' control for iPad users; prefer the existing native SceneKit viewer on iPad where the web SceneView is marginal. References: https://doc.arcgis.com/en/arcgis-online/reference/scene-viewer-requirements.htm and https://developers.arcgis.com/javascript/latest/system-requirements/index.html

findings.principle: Esri's Experience Builder guidance for small and medium screens: auto layouts 'may not handle complex widget arrangements well'; 'Start with the large-screen layout, then work on smaller layouts' using custom layouts per device class; 'Stretching many widgets can overwhelm small screens'; use percentage units 'for adaptive screen sizes that scale on tablets and phones'; and verify with live view at multiple widths.
findings.applicability: Define explicit ERIS breakpoints with distinct compositions rather than fluidly shrinking the desktop split view: desktop (>=1024px) two-pane split view with side detail panel; iPad portrait (768-1023px) full-height map with a bottom sheet or a List/Map segmented control; phone (<768px) list-first with a single map tab. Test the coordinator triage screen and the GISA form at each width on real iPads.

patterns.pattern: Synchronized split view (list + map) with bidirectional highlight
patterns.whenToUse: Desktop and iPad landscape screens where users scan and triage many geolocated records (Baymard: 95% map engagement in split view vs 35% when the map is a hidden toggle).
patterns.erisApplication: Coordinator triage and chief routing queues: left pane is a sortable/filterable incident list with status chips; right pane is the map. Hover/select a row -> marker highlights and map pans (flash, no forced zoom); click a marker -> row scrolls into view and highlights; the selected record's detail opens in a docked panel, not a modal.

patterns.pattern: Map extent as an explicit filter ('Filter list to map area')
patterns.whenToUse: When users narrow a large set geographically; keep it opt-in so panning to look at context does not silently drop rows from the list.
patterns.erisApplication: A toggle above the incident list applies the current map extent as a spatial filter to the list and to the status-count indicators; show a 'Showing 12 of 87 in view' caption and a 'Clear map filter' affordance. Persist the toggle per user.

patterns.pattern: Full-screen map + nonmodal bottom sheet, with 'Open full record' escaping to a page
patterns.whenToUse: Phones and iPad portrait, where there is no room for two panes and the user needs geographic context while reading a summary (NN/g; Calcite block-end Sheet).
patterns.erisApplication: Tapping an incident marker opens a partial-height sheet showing ID, route/postmile, priority, status, reporter, first photo thumbnail and two actions ('Open full report', 'Route/Assign'). The sheet has a close button, Back dismisses it, it never stacks, and the GISA form and approval flow always open as full pages.

patterns.pattern: List-first with map as secondary tab (hide the map by default)
patterns.whenToUse: Phone-width screens, task queues where the primary question is 'what needs my action next' rather than 'where is it', and any workflow step that must be completable without a map (Esri mobile dashboard guidance: one map at most, disable popups on operational layers; W3C: provide equivalent list).
patterns.erisApplication: Phone home for coordinators and reviewers is a list grouped by status with count chips; a 'Map' tab shows only the incident layer; reviewer approval and admin user management never show a map.

patterns.pattern: Collapsible start-side panel for layers, legend and filters that becomes a bottom sheet on narrow viewports
patterns.whenToUse: Whenever the map has more than one operational layer or user-controllable overlays (Calcite Shell Panel / Sheet adaptive pattern).
patterns.erisApplication: An action bar on the map's left edge opens a panel with instant-effect layer toggles ('Show closed incidents', 'Show assessment routes', 'Show evidence photos') and a legend that lists only visible, in-scale operational symbols; on phones the same content renders as a block-end sheet.

patterns.pattern: Scale-dependent clustering with count labels and cluster-to-list drill-down
patterns.whenToUse: Only at zoom levels where incident markers overlap (statewide/district); never at site scale (Esri: clustering is a de-clutter technique, not analysis).
patterns.erisApplication: Cluster incident pins above district scale with abbreviated counts; tapping a cluster zooms in or lists its incidents in the side panel/sheet; clustering is off on the assessment site map so evidence photo markers and observation points keep exact positions.

patterns.pattern: Numbered evidence photo markers linked to form sections
patterns.whenToUse: Long technical forms with georeferenced photos, where reviewers need to relate each photo to a location and to the question it supports (Field Maps attachment elements; AttachmentsContent preview).
patterns.erisApplication: In the GISA form each photo block sits beside its question, is conditionally shown, and can require a minimum count; photos are resized client-side (~960x1280) and plotted on the site map as numbered thumbnail markers; tapping a marker highlights the corresponding form section and opens the full-size photo; the reviewer view shows the same numbered markers with thumbnails in the detail panel.

patterns.pattern: Progressive 3D: capability gate, quality control, and 2D fallback
patterns.whenToUse: Any WebGL2 scene view offered to iPad or phone users (Scene Viewer and Maps SDK requirements; SceneView qualityProfile guidance).
patterns.erisApplication: Show the 3D terrain/cross-section scene only after a WebGL2 and memory check passes; leave qualityProfile on auto but expose a 'Quality: Auto / Low' control; never auto-load 3D on phones; show progress and a timeout that falls back to the 2D map plus a static cross-section image; on iPad prefer the native SceneKit viewer where available.

patterns.pattern: Selection-driven detail panel with empty state
patterns.whenToUse: Dashboards and queues where context depends on a selected record (Esri: selection-based display; render only when a selection exists).
patterns.erisApplication: The right-hand detail panel in the triage/routing views renders only for the selected incident or assessment, with an empty-state prompt otherwise; it shows the record's photos (preview thumbnails), status history and routing actions, and stays a docked panel so list, filters and map remain visible.

patterns.pattern: Status encoded by shape + color + text, with a minimal operational legend
patterns.whenToUse: Every map and list where records carry priority and workflow status (NN/g direct labeling / color-alone; Esri legend guidance).
patterns.erisApplication: Priority uses marker shape/glyph and a short label; workflow status uses a restrained palette plus a text chip in list rows and detail; the legend lists only these operational symbols and omits basemap/reference layers, updating as toggles and scale change.

antiPatterns: Hiding the map behind a 'Map view' toggle or separate tab on desktop/iPad landscape (Baymard: 65% of users never found or engaged it).
Presenting results or record detail in a modal overlay that hides sort/filter controls, or adding a third vertical filter column that crowds the split view.
Stacking bottom sheets, or placing the GISA form, routing decisions or approvals inside a bottom sheet (NN/g: short interactions only, never stack, always a close button).
Relying on map popups to reach records on phones where small features are hard to tap; more than one map or many operational layers on the phone view (Esri mobile dashboard guidance).
Legends that list every layer including basemap/reference data, or that keep showing layers the user has toggled off or that are out of scale range.
Encoding priority or status with color alone in markers, chips or charts.
Layer toggles that need a Save/Apply button, or toggle labels phrased as questions.
Clustering at site/assessment scale where exact evidence positions matter, or deriving status counts from clusters (Esri: clustering is not analysis).
Uploading full-resolution photos from iPads without client-side resizing, and detaching photos from the form question they evidence.
Letting the desktop layout shrink fluidly to phone width instead of designing per-breakpoint compositions; stretching many widgets on small screens.
Auto-loading the 3D scene on every device, forcing qualityProfile to high, or offering no 2D fallback when WebGL2/memory is insufficient or loading stalls.
Making the map the only way to reach a record or complete a step (no synchronized list equivalent, markers not keyboard-reachable).
Map controls and list rows smaller than 24x24 CSS px (44 px on touch) or with no spacing between adjacent targets.
One shared mega-dashboard for all roles, more than two persistent notification banners, and heavy multi-hue color use across indicators and charts.
